bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Cybersecurity & Information Security — Increased reliance on technology exposes the organisation to cybersecurity threats, potential service disruption and data breaches. Managed through a risk-based, layered cybersecurity framework of policies, standards and procedures; continuous threat monitoring, threat intelligence and incident response; regular security assessments and vulnerability management; employee security awareness as a human layer of defence; and cyber resilience and recovery capabilities so critical services can be restored quickly after an incident.
- Data Privacy — Non-compliance with contractual and regulatory data privacy requirements can lead to fines, litigation and reputational damage. Privacy policies, standards and controls are being strengthened across the Personal Data lifecycle, with DPDP governance, processes and accountability mechanisms being established under an ongoing DPDP Act, 2023 readiness programme, plus employee awareness and third-party privacy assessments. The BRSR material-issues table separately flags 'Privacy and Data Security' as a risk requiring regular assessment of technology and cyber security to prevent breaches of sensitive business and stakeholder information.
- Geopolitical instability — Global geopolitical instability can impact safety, mobility and business continuity - directly relevant for a group operating across 28 countries and five continents. Management notes FY 2025-26 geopolitical tensions tested the resilience of the global travel ecosystem; mitigation rests on continuous global monitoring to pre-empt disruptions and insurance coverages and contingency plans protecting customers, employees and operations.
- Foreign exchange (currency) volatility — Exposure to currency fluctuations arising from global operations may affect financial performance - structurally significant given the Foreign Exchange business and multi-currency subsidiary base. Mitigated by a robust hedging policy, active monitoring of currency markets and proactive forex management through hedging contracts.
- Regulatory & compliance / licensing — Non-compliance with statutory, regulatory or licensing requirements can disrupt operations and cause reputational damage - a multi-jurisdiction exposure for the Group. A centralised compliance management system monitors and tracks regulatory, statutory and licensing requirements across jurisdictions including timely renewals, supported by periodic governance reviews and stringent monitoring protocols.
- Credit and counterparty recovery — Delayed or inadequate recoveries from customers and counterparties may adversely impact liquidity and operations. Mitigated through a comprehensive client policy for all transactions and financial evaluations of major clients and partners by the finance team to ensure risk-resilient engagements.
- Environmental and climate change / weather disruption — Natural calamities and adverse weather conditions can impact travel operations and logistics; management cites weather-related disruptions among the FY 2025-26 pressures on the travel ecosystem. Addressed through policies to assess and analyse environmental impact scenarios and strategic adaptability to preserve resilience in operations and travel planning.
- Conduct, human rights and anti-bribery exposure — The BRSR material-issues table identifies Human Rights and Anti-Corruption and Anti-Bribery as risks: frequent regulatory change makes ethical and fair employment practices harder to sustain, and violations of state laws or company rules can carry severe financial, legal and reputational consequences and loss of goodwill. All business operations are under strict monitoring to prevent human rights violations, with robust monitoring and compliance mechanisms to align operations with company values and norms.

outlook.body:
- Reinvention as the operating frame: anticipating change rather than adapting to it, redesigning the portfolio around emerging travel trends, deploying AI to empower people, pioneering frictionless foreign exchange and strengthening a diversified business model to thrive in any environment.
- Follow the customer rather than the market: reshape the holiday portfolio early in response to shorter booking windows, easier visa access and a preference for destinations offering greater certainty, rather than waiting for trends to settle.
- Use portfolio diversification as the shock absorber - the Group states geopolitical disruption was concentrated (Desert Adventures in the Middle East and the UAE business of DEI) rather than broad-based, allowing the wider portfolio to keep progressing.
- Focus management effort only on controllables: allocating capital wisely, prioritising the right customers and markets, remaining invested in technology, making prudent investments and maintaining disciplined cost management, while accepting geopolitics, airspace closures and exchange-rate movements as outside its control.
- Broaden the B2C product set beyond conventional itineraries - event-led and sports tourism, experiential holidays, culinary and cultural journeys, wildlife expeditions, self-drive vacations and premium rail experiences.
- Scale purpose-led and pilgrimage travel as a year-round rather than seasonal opportunity, deepening the Bhakti and Darshans portfolios across Char Dham, Jyotirlingas, Ramayan Yatras, Kashi-Prayagraj-Ayodhya-Bodh Gaya and the Kailash Mansarovar Yatra, backed by terrain-specific insurance.
- Expand domestically where preferences shift, including extending the Bhutan charter programme, curated festival departures and strengthened offerings for senior travellers.
- Grow B2B through Corporate Travel client-base and international footprint expansion, large-format MICE assignments, and a Destination Management Services presence across 28 countries used to offset regional volatility.
- Invest in a digital ecosystem across B2C (Tacy Chat Bot and Voice Bot in English and Hindi, website and app upgrades, AI Agent Assist, QC Bot) and B2B (Travart for India inbound, TravelOne for corporate travel, ECONNECT for Asian Trails, Premiere for Allied TPro, the Customer Service App and Tour Pe for MICE).
- Institutionalise customer measurement through the Customer Experience Index (CXI), a global customer-satisfaction model capturing Ease, Satisfaction and Net Promoter Scores across every key touchpoint, supported by Customer First Awards.
- Strengthen the customer proposition against travel disruption with industry-first products - TravSure travel assurance covering war and war-like conditions, airspace closures and 24x7 support, and a first-of-its-kind Visa Rejection Cover.
- Push forex from digitised transactions to genuinely frictionless services - Borderless Travel Card extended to 28 currencies with Google Pay tap-and-pay, the relaunched One Currency Zero Markup Card for frequent travellers, and the Study Buddy Card scaled through partnerships with leading education NBFCs.
- Balance operational responsiveness with prudent capital allocation so the Group can stay resilient in an uncertain global environment while continuing to invest in strategic growth opportunities.
outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: TCIL is an asset-light travel and financial-services group with no manufacturing plants; its physical expansion is concentrated in the Leisure Hospitality and Resorts business (Sterling Holiday Resorts Limited and Nature Trails) and in distribution/office footprint. Sterling's expansion is guided by an asset-right philosophy that combines ownership with management-led growth: 62% of the portfolio operates through owned, leased and revenue-share properties, generating operating leverage, while 38% comprises managed properties that enable rapid expansion into high-growth Tier II and Tier III destinations with lower capital intensity. During FY 2025-26 room inventory grew more than 17%, and when excessive rainfall and landslides hit Northern India in Q2 the Company redeployed internal resources to accelerate expansion, launching seven new resorts in a single quarter. Key additions and portfolio enhancements included Sterling Arka Suites, Puri - Sterling's first all-suite luxury resort with 46 keys, which commenced revenue operations in the third quarter and achieved stabilised performance by year-end; 32 suites added at Sterling Kodai Valley; 51 rooms added at Sterling Munnar alongside an upgrade of 38% of that resort's inventory; refurbishment and infrastructure upgrades at Sterling Kodai Lake, Sterling Nainital and Sterling Yercaud; the Katha restaurant introduced at Jaisinghgarh, Udaipur to expand the F&B offering; and Sterling Mount Olive, Gangtok, a second upscale property in Sikkim. Early presence was established in high-growth leisure markets including Ayodhya, Malampuzha, Bokaro, Madurai, Karwar and Dehradun (two properties). The stated forward plan takes the ecosystem from 78 resorts, 65 locations and 3,798 rooms currently (as of June 2026) to 95 resorts, 75 locations and 4,800 rooms in FY 2026-27. Alongside network expansion, Sterling is investing in selective upgrades across the existing portfolio to improve room inventory, guest experience and revenue potential, and in a technology stack covering AI-enabled guest engagement, intelligent revenue management systems and integrated hospitality platforms. The AR bundle contains a 'Capital commitments' note heading (capital expenditure contracted for at the end of the reporting period but not recognised as liabilities) at pages 158 and 227, but no rupee figure accompanies it in the material supplied, so no capex quantum is recorded.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- Structural Indian demand: a young, aspirational population, rising incomes, expanding middle-class households and rapid urbanisation broadening the travel consumer base; long-term projections indicate India could add around 140 mn middle-income households by 2030.
- Passport penetration as an outbound leading indicator - more than 143 million passports issued cumulatively between March 2014 and March 2026, including over 1.38 mn in FY 2025-26 alone.
- The World Economic Forum estimate that middle-class and affluent consumers will account for 93% of India's total consumer spending by 2036, up from 80% in 2026.
- Demand evolved rather than weakened - shorter booking windows, easier visa access and a preference for destinations offering certainty; short-haul delivered 17% growth while long-haul stayed resilient despite elevated airfares, constrained airline capacity and longer visa processing timelines.
- Two distinct halves to FY 2025-26: the first nine months saw stable conditions with 7% revenue growth and marginally improved EBITDA, while Q4 revenue fell 10% year-on-year to Rs 17,707 mn on the Middle East overhang, cost headwinds and a travel market recalibrating in real time - producing 3.3% growth for the full year.
- Middle East disruption is material to global travel because the region accounts for ~5% of global international arrivals and 14% of global international transit traffic; Q1 2026 Middle East arrivals fell 14% while Europe and Africa each grew 4%, Asia-Pacific 3% and the Americas 2%.
- WTTC forecasts Travel & Tourism GDP to grow 3.2% in CY 2026, ahead of projected global economic growth of 2.4%, contributing ~US$12 trillion and supporting 376 million jobs; over the next decade the sector is projected to grow 3.6% annually versus 2.4% for the wider economy.
- Cost headwinds to travel demand: the World Bank projects Brent crude to average US$94 per barrel in 2026, 36% above 2025 levels, and global inflation to rise to 4.0% in 2026 from 3.3% in 2025, potentially pushing travellers toward shorter-haul or regional journeys, flexible arrangements and destinations offering reliable connectivity and value.
- Forex industry demand moderated: total LRS remittances fell 2% to US$28.98 billion, with travel down 3% to US$16.44 billion and studies abroad down 21% to US$2.31 billion, while the 'Others' category rose 12% - a softer industry backdrop the company says it navigated through product and partnership initiatives.
- Structural support for forex from rising cross-border trade, FDI flows, NRI remittances, corporate globalisation, India's position as the world's largest recipient of remittances, RBI measures in 2026 to encourage fresh FCNR(B) deposits, and a US$250,000 per-year LRS limit for resident individuals.
- Digital transformation of the forex market - digital platforms, mobile-first services, electronic execution and automated KYC and compliance improving accessibility and transaction efficiency, alongside greater corporate use of currency swaps, forwards and options.
- Indian domestic tourism as the principal engine: more than 4.13 billion domestic tourist visits in 2025 versus around 2.94 billion in 2024, supported by Tier II and Tier III participation, improved road and regional air connectivity and preference for short-haul, experience-led travel.
- Inbound India remains below potential - 20.57 million International Tourist Arrivals in 2024 (14.85% above 2019) with FTAs of 9.95 million, and WTTC estimating international visitors spend an average of 18.5 days in India, among the longest stays globally.
- Macro backdrop: India's real GDP grew 7.7% in FY 2025-26, with the IMF projecting 6.4% in FY 2026-27 and 6.7% in FY 2027-28; global growth is projected at 3.0% in CY 2026 recovering to 3.4% in CY 2027.
- Major international events including the FIFA World Cup 2026 are expected to generate additional travel demand, particularly across host markets and neighbouring destinations.
- Travel segment EBIT was pressured by the heightened geopolitical environment - disruption across key international markets and the resulting pressure on travel flows and operating costs - even as total travel revenue grew 4%.
- For travel businesses generally, management expects diversification of source markets and routes, flexibility in offerings and speed of response to changes in connectivity, costs and traveller behaviour to become increasingly important.

Global geopolitical instability can impact safety, mobility and business continuity - directly relevant for a group operating across 28 countries and five continents. Mitigated by a robust hedging policy, active monitoring of currency markets and proactive forex management through hedging contracts.

Non-compliance with statutory, regulatory or licensing requirements can disrupt operations and cause reputational damage - a multi-jurisdiction exposure for the Group. currentContext.expansion: TCIL is an asset-light travel and financial-services group with no manufacturing plants; its physical expansion is concentrated in the Leisure Hospitality and Resorts business (Sterling Holiday Resorts Limited and Nature Trails) and in distribution/office footprint. Sterling's expansion is guided by an asset-right philosophy that combines ownership with management-led growth: 62% of the portfolio operates through owned, leased and revenue-share properties, generating operating leverage, while 38% comprises managed properties that enable rapid expansion into high-growth Tier II and Tier III destinations with lower capital intensity. During FY 2025-26 room inventory grew more than 17%, and when excessive rainfall and landslides hit Northern India in Q2 the Company redeployed internal resources to accelerate expansion, launching seven new resorts in a single quarter. Key additions and portfolio enhancements included Sterling Arka Suites, Puri - Sterling's first all-suite luxury resort with 46 keys, which commenced revenue operations in the third quarter and achieved stabilised performance by year-end; 32 suites added at Sterling Kodai Valley; 51 rooms added at Sterling Munnar alongside an upgrade of 38% of that resort's inventory; refurbishment and infrastructure upgrades at Sterling Kodai Lake, Sterling Nainital and Sterling Yercaud; the Katha restaurant introduced at Jaisinghgarh, Udaipur to expand the F&B offering; and Sterling Mount Olive, Gangtok, a second upscale property in Sikkim. Early presence was established in high-growth leisure markets including Ayodhya, Malampuzha, Bokaro, Madurai, Karwar and Dehradun (two properties). The stated forward plan takes the ecosystem from 78 resorts, 65 locations and 3,798 rooms currently (as of June 2026) to 95 resorts, 75 locations and 4,800 rooms in FY 2026-27. Alongside network expansion, Sterling is investing in selective upgrades across the existing portfolio to improve room inventory, guest experience and revenue potential, and in a technology stack covering AI-enabled guest engagement, intelligent revenue management systems and integrated hospitality platforms. The AR bundle contains a 'Capital commitments' note heading (capital expenditure contracted for at the end of the reporting period but not recognised as liabilities) at pages 158 and 227, but no rupee figure accompanies it in the material supplied, so no capex quantum is recorded.

one_liner.title: One Liner (RHP)
one_liner.body: Thomas Cook (India) Limited is an integrated travel and travel-related financial services enterprise spanning travel, foreign exchange, payment solutions, destination management, hospitality, travel technology and digital imaging, with operations across 28 countries.

business_model.title: What they do
business_model.body: TCIL operates a portfolio of B2C and B2B brands across four reported businesses: Travel and Related Services (leisure holidays, corporate travel, MICE and destination management), Financial Services (retail and wholesale foreign exchange, multi-currency prepaid cards, outward remittances and forex advisory), Leisure Hospitality and Resorts, and Digital Imaging Solutions. It serves leisure travellers, families, corporates, students, institutions, government and quasi-government bodies, NRIs and financial partners through an omnichannel network of retail branches, franchisee and agent touchpoints, airport counters and digital platforms. Headquartered in India and backed by the Fairfax Group, it describes itself as having built one of the largest travel service networks in the Asia-Pacific region.

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- Structural Indian demand: a young, aspirational population, rising incomes, expanding middle-class households and rapid urbanisation broadening the travel consumer base; long-term projections indicate India could add around 140 mn middle-income households by 2030.
- Passport penetration as an outbound leading indicator - more than 143 million passports issued cumulatively between March 2014 and March 2026, including over 1.38 mn in FY 2025-26 alone.
- The World Economic Forum estimate that middle-class and affluent consumers will account for 93% of India's total consumer spending by 2036, up from 80% in 2026.
- Demand evolved rather than weakened - shorter booking windows, easier visa access and a preference for destinations offering certainty; short-haul delivered 17% growth while long-haul stayed resilient despite elevated airfares, constrained airline capacity and longer visa processing timelines.
- Two distinct halves to FY 2025-26: the first nine months saw stable conditions with 7% revenue growth and marginally improved EBITDA, while Q4 revenue fell 10% year-on-year to Rs 17,707 mn on the Middle East overhang, cost headwinds and a travel market recalibrating in real time - producing 3.3% growth for the full year.
- Middle East disruption is material to global travel because the region accounts for ~5% of global international arrivals and 14% of global international transit traffic; Q1 2026 Middle East arrivals fell 14% while Europe and Africa each grew 4%, Asia-Pacific 3% and the Americas 2%.
- WTTC forecasts Travel & Tourism GDP to grow 3.2% in CY 2026, ahead of projected global economic growth of 2.4%, contributing ~US$12 trillion and supporting 376 million jobs; over the next decade the sector is projected to grow 3.6% annually versus 2.4% for the wider economy.
- Cost headwinds to travel demand: the World Bank projects Brent crude to average US$94 per barrel in 2026, 36% above 2025 levels, and global inflation to rise to 4.0% in 2026 from 3.3% in 2025, potentially pushing travellers toward shorter-haul or regional journeys, flexible arrangements and destinations offering reliable connectivity and value.
- Forex industry demand moderated: total LRS remittances fell 2% to US$28.98 billion, with travel down 3% to US$16.44 billion and studies abroad down 21% to US$2.31 billion, while the 'Others' category rose 12% - a softer industry backdrop the company says it navigated through product and partnership initiatives.
- Structural support for forex from rising cross-border trade, FDI flows, NRI remittances, corporate globalisation, India's position as the world's largest recipient of remittances, RBI measures in 2026 to encourage fresh FCNR(B) deposits, and a US$250,000 per-year LRS limit for resident individuals.
- Digital transformation of the forex market - digital platforms, mobile-first services, electronic execution and automated KYC and compliance improving accessibility and transaction efficiency, alongside greater corporate use of currency swaps, forwards and options.
- Indian domestic tourism as the principal engine: more than 4.13 billion domestic tourist visits in 2025 versus around 2.94 billion in 2024, supported by Tier II and Tier III participation, improved road and regional air connectivity and preference for short-haul, experience-led travel.
- Inbound India remains below potential - 20.57 million International Tourist Arrivals in 2024 (14.85% above 2019) with FTAs of 9.95 million, and WTTC estimating international visitors spend an average of 18.5 days in India, among the longest stays globally.
- Macro backdrop: India's real GDP grew 7.7% in FY 2025-26, with the IMF projecting 6.4% in FY 2026-27 and 6.7% in FY 2027-28; global growth is projected at 3.0% in CY 2026 recovering to 3.4% in CY 2027.
- Major international events including the FIFA World Cup 2026 are expected to generate additional travel demand, particularly across host markets and neighbouring destinations.
- Travel segment EBIT was pressured by the heightened geopolitical environment - disruption across key international markets and the resulting pressure on travel flows and operating costs - even as total travel revenue grew 4%.
- For travel businesses generally, management expects diversification of source markets and routes, flexibility in offerings and speed of response to changes in connectivity, costs and traveller behaviour to become increasingly important.

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: TCIL is an asset-light travel and financial-services group with no manufacturing plants; its physical expansion is concentrated in the Leisure Hospitality and Resorts business (Sterling Holiday Resorts Limited and Nature Trails) and in distribution/office footprint. Sterling's expansion is guided by an asset-right philosophy that combines ownership with management-led growth: 62% of the portfolio operates through owned, leased and revenue-share properties, generating operating leverage, while 38% comprises managed properties that enable rapid expansion into high-growth Tier II and Tier III destinations with lower capital intensity. During FY 2025-26 room inventory grew more than 17%, and when excessive rainfall and landslides hit Northern India in Q2 the Company redeployed internal resources to accelerate expansion, launching seven new resorts in a single quarter. Key additions and portfolio enhancements included Sterling Arka Suites, Puri - Sterling's first all-suite luxury resort with 46 keys, which commenced revenue operations in the third quarter and achieved stabilised performance by year-end; 32 suites added at Sterling Kodai Valley; 51 rooms added at Sterling Munnar alongside an upgrade of 38% of that resort's inventory; refurbishment and infrastructure upgrades at Sterling Kodai Lake, Sterling Nainital and Sterling Yercaud; the Katha restaurant introduced at Jaisinghgarh, Udaipur to expand the F&B offering; and Sterling Mount Olive, Gangtok, a second upscale property in Sikkim. Early presence was established in high-growth leisure markets including Ayodhya, Malampuzha, Bokaro, Madurai, Karwar and Dehradun (two properties). The stated forward plan takes the ecosystem from 78 resorts, 65 locations and 3,798 rooms currently (as of June 2026) to 95 resorts, 75 locations and 4,800 rooms in FY 2026-27. Alongside network expansion, Sterling is investing in selective upgrades across the existing portfolio to improve room inventory, guest experience and revenue potential, and in a technology stack covering AI-enabled guest engagement, intelligent revenue management systems and integrated hospitality platforms. The AR bundle contains a 'Capital commitments' note heading (capital expenditure contracted for at the end of the reporting period but not recognised as liabilities) at pages 158 and 227, but no rupee figure accompanies it in the material supplied, so no capex quantum is recorded.

themes.title: Hospitality & travel up-cycle
themes.need: Q1FY27 split hotels from airlines. INDHOTEL delivered a 17th consecutive record quarter - consolidated revenue INR 2,419cr (+15%), EBITDA INR 753cr at 31.1%, standalone occupancy jumping to 82% from 76% on a 41.8% standalone EBITDA margin, and asset-light management-fee income INR 168cr (+26%) - with management now framing the West-Asia war as a NET tailwind because outbound travel stays home; leisure RevPAR (Rajasthan/Goa) ran up high-20s. Airlines got the mirror image: INDIGO's EBITDAR margin collapsed from 28.0% to 15.6% on blended ATF of ~INR 140-150/litre versus INR 85-90 pre-war (fuel CASK +~80% YoY), leaving yield as the only defence. MHRIL shows domestic leisure premiumisation is real - Keystone average unit realisation +73% to INR 14.4 lakh on stable gross sales. LEMONTREE/CHALET/SAMHI/THELEELA ride the same occupancy-led room cycle; TRAVELFOOD/TBOTEK/DREAMFOLKS remain levered to airport PAX and B2B travel.
themes.driver: Occupancy-led (not rate-led) RevPAR compounding plus INDHOTEL's Ginger conversion cadence stepping 15->20->25->40 per quarter through FY27; for airlines the swing is INDIGO's guided Q2 PRASK growth of 'more than 25%' on flattish capacity against ATF cracks.
